summary: Defines textual conventions for MIB modules that record performance history in 15 minute intervals. Different modules can reuse them. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 3593.

eli5.summary: This sets the way a gauge keeps a record of how the last few hours went, saving a score for each 15 minute slot.

subtitle: Standard conventions for tracking device performance in regular intervals.

tldr.problem: Network equipment needs to track performance history in a consistent way, and many systems use 15-minute intervals to record measurements like error counts and traffic levels.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines reusable textual conventions (data type definitions) for MIB modules that want to store performance data bucketed into 15-minute time periods, with support for tracking both current and historical measurements.
tldr.outcome: Network managers can now use a standard set of performance tracking definitions across different equipment, avoiding duplication and making their MIBs easier to write and maintain. This RFC was updated by RFC 3593.

today: RFC 2493 is a Proposed Standard that defines the convention itself. It was updated by RFC 3593, which provides enhancements to these textual conventions. The base conventions remain in use wherever 15-minute performance history is tracked in network management.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2493 defines a set of textual conventions for MIB modules that need to record performance history using 15-minute intervals. In network management, performance history is commonly tracked in two ways: an agent can count events continuously and the manager can calculate history, or the agent can bucket events into fixed time periods.

Telecommunications equipment often uses the bucket method with 15-minute intervals. This RFC provides standard definitions that any MIB module can reuse instead of defining its own. These textual conventions make MIB modules easier to write and read by providing standardized, named types with clear semantics.
sections.eli5: Different network boxes all keep track of what happened every 15 minutes. Instead of each one making up its own numbers and names, this says what everybody should call them and what they mean.

sections.title: The Three Performance Counters
sections.content:
The RFC defines three textual conventions for performance measurement counters:

PerfCurrentCount tracks a measurement during the current 15-minute interval. It starts at zero and increments as events occur. When the interval ends, this value is stored in history and the counter resets.

PerfIntervalCount stores measurements from completed 15-minute intervals. A system keeps a history of n intervals (where 1 ≤ n ≤ 96). When a new interval completes, the oldest interval is discarded and all others shift back one position, with the current count becoming the most recent history entry.

PerfTotalCount aggregates measurements across all previous valid intervals, providing a sum of completed interval counts. This is optional but useful for getting cumulative statistics.
sections.eli5: The current counter keeps track right now. The history counters keep track of the past few hours. The total counter adds everything up for you.

sections.title: Design Assumptions
sections.content:
The RFC assumes that an agent supporting these conventions will:

  • Maintain a 15-minute based history with n intervals of data (n can be 1 to 96)
  • Keep separate tables for the current interval, historical intervals, and total aggregates
  • Handle cases where valid data is unavailable (for example, when a proxy manager loses connection to the actual device)
  • Provide related objects to track elapsed time in the current interval and the number of valid historical intervals available

These assumptions let managers query performance data in a standard way across different types of equipment without needing to understand device-specific implementations.
sections.eli5: Every device keeps maybe the last 96 fifteen-minute scores, plus a running total. If the device can't talk to the real thing, it marks those scores as missing.

sections.title: Notes on Time and Interval Counting
sections.content:
The xyzTimeElapsed counter tracks seconds into the current 15-minute interval (maximum 899 seconds). If the agent's time-of-day clock adjusts, this value may occasionally exceed the maximum, in which case the agent returns the maximum value.

The xyzValidIntervals counter tracks how many historical intervals contain valid data, constrained by the total number n. When the system first starts or when the agent cannot reach the actual device, this count may be less than n.

The xyzInvalidIntervals counter records the number of intervals within the valid range that have no data available, typically seen in proxy situations where communication is temporarily lost.
sections.eli5: If the device's clock gets bumped by a second or two, we just cap the current counter at its max. If some past 15-minute chunks are missing, we remember which ones.
